result: GluA4 deletion causes an ~80% reduction in mossy fiber to granule cell (MF→GC) synaptic transmission with slower EPSC decay kinetics, demonstrating that GluA4 is indispensable for fast neurotransmission at MF→GC synapses.
evaluation: Claims C1, C21, C22 present experimental data from Figure 1B-C showing statistically significant reduction in EPSC amplitude (13.4 ± 1.1 pA vs. 76.2 ± 7.5 pA; p < 0.0001) and slower decay kinetics (3.1 ± 0.3 ms vs. 1.8 ± 0.2 ms; p < 0.001) in GluA4-KO mice. The conclusion (C33, C102) that GluA4 is indispensable for fast MF→GC transmission is well-supported by these data and consistent with the known properties of GluA4-containing AMPARs.

result: GluA4 deletion does not affect synaptic transmission at other cerebellar synapses (MF→GoC, PF→GoC, PF→PC), indicating selective impairment at MF→GC synapses.
evaluation: Claims C23-C31 present experimental data from Figures 1D-L and supplementary figures showing no significant differences in EPSC amplitudes, decay kinetics, spontaneous EPSCs, or paired-pulse ratios at MF→GoC, PF→GoC, and PF→PC synapses between WT and GluA4-KO mice. This demonstrates the specificity of the GluA4 effect to MF→GC synapses and rules out general cerebellar dysfunction.

result: GluA4-KO granule cells show increased excitability under control conditions due to reduced tonic GABAergic inhibition, as evidenced by higher firing frequencies that normalize in the presence of bicuculline and reduced bicuculline-sensitive conductance.
evaluation: Claims C34-C42 present converging experimental evidence from Figure 2 showing: (1) increased firing in GluA4-KO GCs under control conditions (linear mixed effects analysis: p < 0.001), (2) normalization of input-output relationship with bicuculline (p = 0.43), (3) differential effects of bicuculline on gain and rheobase between genotypes (ANOVA p = 0.041), and (4) reduced tonic inhibitory conductance (39.0 ± 9.6 pS/pF vs. 83.0 ± 13.3 pS/pF, p = 0.022). The conclusion (C47) that reduced tonic inhibition compensates for reduced excitatory input is well-supported.

result: The reduction in tonic inhibition in GluA4-KO GCs is associated with lower α6 GABAAR expression levels, while phasic inhibition remains unaltered.
evaluation: Claims C44-C46 present experimental data from Figure 2—figure supplement 2 showing reduced α6 GABAAR levels by Western blot and no differences in spontaneous IPSC properties. The inference (C112) that reduced α6 GABAAR expression contributes to reduced tonic inhibition is reasonable given the known role of α6 GABAARs in mediating tonic inhibition in GCs (C43). However, the Western blot shows only a modest reduction and the mechanistic link could be strengthened with additional experiments.

result: Reduced tonic inhibition in GluA4-KO GCs augments synaptic depolarization, as demonstrated by differential effects of bicuculline on EPSP amplitudes between WT and GluA4-KO mice.
evaluation: Claims C48-C53 present experimental data from Figure 3 showing that while both EPSCs and EPSPs are reduced in GluA4-KO GCs, the relative reduction is smaller for EPSPs (69.4% vs. 80.6%, p < 0.001). Bicuculline increases EPSP amplitudes in WT but not in GluA4-KO GCs (ANOVA drug × genotype: F = 8.00, p = 0.005), demonstrating that shunting inhibition normally reduces postsynaptic depolarization in WT but is absent in GluA4-KO. This provides strong evidence for the compensatory role of reduced tonic inhibition.

result: GluA4-KO granule cells show reduced spike frequency, increased spike delay, and decreased reliability during high-frequency mossy fiber stimulation, demonstrating that GluA4-containing AMPARs control the timing and reliability of EPSP-spike coupling.
evaluation: Claims C54-C59 present experimental data from Figure 4 showing: (1) reduced firing frequency in GluA4-KO GCs (ANOVA genotype: F = 23.48; p < 0.0001), (2) fewer spiking cells, (3) longer spike delay (ANOVA genotype: F = 26.26; p < 0.0001), and (4) modeling data showing increased EPSP summation requirement. These converging lines of evidence strongly support the conclusion that GluA4 is critical for temporal precision and reliability of GC spike output during high-frequency transmission.

result: GluA4-KO mice show enhanced NMDAR-mediated transmission at MF→GC synapses, with larger NMDAR-EPSCs and increased cumulative charge during train stimulation, likely due to increased presynaptic release sites.
evaluation: Claims C60-C63 present experimental data from Figure 5 showing: (1) larger isolated NMDAR-EPSCs in GluA4-KO (37.2 ± 2.1 pA vs. 27.5 ± 2.1 pA; p = 0.0026), (2) statistical moments analysis indicating increased release sites without changes in release probability or quantal size, (3) reduced AMPAR-mediated charge (p < 0.0001), and (4) increased NMDAR-mediated charge (p = 0.0063) during 100 Hz trains. The data support enhanced NMDAR transmission, though the mechanistic interpretation regarding release sites could benefit from additional validation.

result: Computational modeling reveals that reduced tonic inhibition and enhanced NMDAR transmission each contribute ~20% to the maximum spiking frequency of GluA4-KO GCs, but these compensatory mechanisms are insufficient to fully compensate for the pronounced impairment of AMPAR-mediated excitation.
evaluation: Claims C64-C70 present modeling results from Figure 5 showing: (1) reduced firing frequencies in the KO model across all MF input frequencies, (2) ~44% reduced maximum firing frequency, (3) increased spike delay, (4) individual contributions of ~20% each from reduced inhibition and enhanced NMDAR transmission, and (5) compromised MF-GC spike synchrony. The modeling is well-constrained by experimental data and provides mechanistic insights into the partial compensation. The conclusion that compensation is insufficient is supported by persistent deficits in the model.

result: Feedforward network modeling shows that GluA4 deletion impairs expansion coding by reducing total variance (coding space) without affecting population sparseness, leading to reduced learning speed across all model parameters.
evaluation: Claims C76-C84 present computational modeling results from Figure 6 showing: (1) similar population sparseness between control and KO models, (2) strongly reduced total variance in the KO model, (3) reduced learning speed across all parameter ranges, (4) GC activity accelerating learning only at high MF correlation and activity levels in the KO model, and (5) total variance (but not sparseness) predicting learning speed. The modeling is based on a published framework (Cayco-Gajic et al., 2017) with parameters scaled according to experimental data, providing strong computational support for impaired expansion coding.

result: GluA4-KO mice show largely intact locomotor coordination during overground walking, with comparable stride lengths, paw trajectories, and interlimb coordination to WT mice, despite minor hyperflexion and a tendency to walk more slowly.
evaluation: Claims C86-C93 present extensive locomotor analysis data from Figure 7 and supplementary figures using the LocoMouse system, showing: (1) no obvious gait ataxia, (2) comparable stride lengths across walking speeds, (3) intact paw trajectories, (4) largely normal vertical paw motion with minor hyperflexion, and (5) similar interlimb coordination with symmetrical trot patterns. The quantitative analysis is comprehensive and includes comparison with ataxic mouse models (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), strongly supporting the conclusion of spared locomotor coordination.

result: GluA4-KO mice completely fail to form associative memories during delay eyeblink conditioning with both visual and whisker stimuli, while showing normal unconditioned responses, demonstrating that GluA4 is required for cerebellum-dependent associative learning independent of CS modality.
evaluation: Claims C94-C99 present behavioral data from Figure 8 showing: (1) similar unconditioned responses between genotypes (p = 0.36), (2) continuous increase in conditioned responses in WT mice, (3) complete absence of CR development in GluA4-KO mice over 10 training sessions with both visual and whisker CS, and (4) no learned eyelid closures in CS-only trials. The use of two different CS modalities strengthens the conclusion that the deficit is not sensory-specific. The complete absence of learning is striking and well-documented.

result: The dissociation between spared locomotor coordination and impaired eyeblink conditioning in GluA4-KO mice suggests that locomotor coordination can be sustained by low levels of GC activity and may rely on effective population sparsening, while associative memory formation may require more complex levels of GC activity and/or synaptic integration.
evaluation: Claims C100, C127, C128 present interpretations of the behavioral dissociation between locomotion and learning. While the experimental observations are well-supported (C105, C106), the mechanistic explanations are largely speculative. The manuscript acknowledges this uncertainty with phrases like "may rely on" and "may require." The modeling results showing maintained sparseness but reduced total variance provide some support, but the specific requirements for locomotion vs. learning remain unclear. Additional experiments would be needed to test these hypotheses directly.

result: The compensatory mechanisms in GluA4-KO GCs (reduced tonic inhibition and enhanced NMDAR transmission) are insufficient to maintain the fidelity of GC output at WT levels, as other AMPAR subunits cannot compensate for the loss of GluA4.
evaluation: Claims C110-C115 synthesize the experimental findings showing: (1) strong reduction in MF→GC EPSCs indicating lack of compensation by other AMPAR subunits, (2) reduced tonic inhibition and enhanced NMDAR transmission as compensatory mechanisms, (3) increased excitability of GluA4-KO GCs, but (4) persistent deficits in spike output fidelity. The conclusion is well-supported by the combined electrophysiological, modeling, and behavioral data. The inference about lack of AMPAR subunit compensation is supported by citations to similar findings in other systems.

result: Speculative mechanisms for the behavioral dissociation include: (1) dense MF activity during locomotion may activate sufficient GCs despite raised threshold, (2) sparse CS representation may not activate enough GCs in GluA4-KO mice, (3) longer spike delay may cause GC spikes to arrive too late to trigger CRs, and (4) altered MF→GC transmission may interfere with PF→PC plasticity.
evaluation: Claims C116-C119, C130, C131 present speculative explanations for the behavioral dissociation, supported by citations to relevant literature. While these hypotheses are plausible and consistent with known properties of cerebellar circuits, they remain untested in the current study. The manuscript appropriately presents these as speculation ("may," "might," "could"). These represent important directions for future work but do not constitute supported results from the current study.

result: The findings support a role for MF→GC synapses in cerebellar associative learning and are consistent with the hypothesis that pattern separation at the cerebellar input layer promotes associative memory formation.
evaluation: Claims C122, C125, C126, C134 present the main conclusions of the study, integrating the electrophysiological, modeling, and behavioral findings. The conclusion that MF→GC synapses are important for associative learning is supported by: (1) selective impairment of MF→GC transmission, (2) impaired expansion coding in the network model, (3) complete absence of eyeblink conditioning, and (4) citations to previous work establishing that eyeblink conditioning occurs in the cerebellum. While the systemic KO model has limitations (acknowledged in the manuscript), the convergent evidence strongly supports this conclusion.

result: Background claims about GluA4 expression, cerebellar anatomy, and circuit function are supported by appropriate citations to previous literature.
evaluation: Claims C6-C20, C27, C39, C43, C71-C75, C108-C109, C120-C121, C123-C125 present background information about GluA4 expression patterns, AMPAR properties, cerebellar anatomy, circuit function, and previous findings in other brain regions. All claims are appropriately supported by citations to relevant literature. These provide necessary context for interpreting the current findings but do not represent novel results from this study.

result: The study demonstrates the importance of GluA4 for cerebellar input layer synaptic function and associative memory formation, providing evidence for an AMPAR code in which different AMPAR subunits serve different roles for synaptic function and learning.
evaluation: Claims C32, C107, C135 present the overarching conclusions of the study. The conclusion that GluA4 is important for cerebellar input layer function and associative learning is strongly supported by the convergent evidence from electrophysiology, modeling, and behavior. The broader conclusion about an AMPAR code (C135) is supported by citation to previous work (Diering and Huganir, 2018) and the current findings add GluA4 in the cerebellum to this framework. The observation of grossly normal cerebellar anatomy (C32) rules out major developmental abnormalities.
